stories.headline: Update: Suspect in Lakewood officer's killing had absconded from parole weeks before shooting
stories.summary:
Gabriel Steven Garcia, 34, the man suspected of killing Lakewood Police Agent Nicholas Graham and wounding three other officers aboard an RTD bus Thursday, had been released from prison to mandatory parole on Sept. 23, according to records reviewed by The Denver Gazette. Garcia had been serving a sentence for first-degree criminal trespass of an inhabited dwelling, and his criminal history included a violent assault on a sheriff's deputy.

Two days after his release, Garcia was listed as a parole absconder. Broomfield police took him into custody on Sept. 28, apparently on a parole warrant, and held him until Oct. 20. The state has not publicly explained the circumstances of that release. Sixteen days later, he was killed in the confrontation with Lakewood officers near West Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard.

The Department of Corrections said it is conducting an internal review of Garcia's supervision. The department had already been reviewing its Community Supervision Tool assessments after a 9News investigation found widespread errors in how parolees were classified. As of Oct. 31, supervisors had reviewed 1,797 assessments and flagged 1,122 for reassessment, with 660 completed. It is unclear whether Garcia's assessment was among those flagged.

Lakewood police said officers recognized the suspect before engaging him but have not explained why they were looking for him. The Gazette has filed open records requests seeking more information.

stories.headline: Update: Mayor Johnston accepts council changes, finalizing Denver's $1.684 billion 2027 budget
stories.summary:
Denver's 2027 budget is officially adopted after Mayor Mike Johnston accepted City Council's amendments Friday, ending months of negotiations over spending priorities amid sluggish revenue growth. On Monday, council had approved five of the 16 amendments its members proposed. Johnston announced his approval in a letter to council.

The amended budget raises funding for the Temporary Rental and Utility Assistance program to $8.5 million, up from the mayor's original $4.5 million proposal. That is still well below the $15.1 million budgeted this year. It also provides about $2 million to offset costs of Denver CARES, the city's detox facility, after no extra money was included for Denver Health and Hospital Authority. The dispute renewed scrutiny of Denver CARES' detention practices after a federal jury found the facility violated two people's Fourth Amendment rights in 2024 and awarded $660,000 in damages. The budget also adds support for businesses affected by construction projects and more staffing for the 911 Emergency Communications Center.

The city projects flat revenue growth of 1.1% next year, or about $17.5 million in additional revenue. To pay for the amendments, Johnston will draw on the contingency reserve, existing departmental budgets and other sources. The contingency falls from 2.06% to 2.01% of General Fund expenditures, just above the 2% charter minimum, or about $33.8 million.

stories.headline: First Watch plans restaurant near Denver International Airport
stories.summary:
National breakfast chain First Watch plans to open a restaurant in northeast Denver near Denver International Airport. Plans submitted to the city by Galloway & Co. in late October show a 3,500-square-foot restaurant at 5773 N. Tower Road, within the Link 56 development. The site covers about 0.84 acres and would include 60 parking spaces.

Link 56 is a 150-acre project at East 56th Avenue and Tower Road, acquired last year by Kensington Development Partners in partnership with U.K.-based IM Properties. Construction is underway on the first phase, which includes a 150,799-square-foot Target, 215 apartments, 170 townhomes and additional retail, with an estimated investment of $235 million. At buildout, the development is expected to have about 250,000 square feet of commercial space, 27 acres of parks and open space, and roughly 2,000 residential units.

First Watch serves breakfast, brunch and lunch at more than 680 restaurants in 33 states and operates more than 10 locations in Colorado, from Colorado Springs to Arvada. German discount grocer Aldi has also been proposed next door at 18453 E. 57th Ave. Representatives for First Watch and Kensington did not respond to requests for comment.

stories.headline: Broncos activate Pat Bryant, place Eyioma Uwazurike on injured reserve
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos activated wide receiver Pat Bryant from injured reserve Saturday, and he will play Sunday against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte. Bryant was hurt Oct. 4 at San Francisco and missed four games, the minimum stay on injured reserve.

Defensive lineman Eyioma Uwazurike moved the other way. He suffered a shoulder injury in last Sunday's 28-24 win over Kansas City and was ruled out Friday. Because he was placed on injured reserve, the starter must miss at least four games. Rookie defensive back Sean Fresch Jr. was promoted from the practice squad to take his roster spot. Fresch had already been elevated the maximum three times this season, so a promotion to the 53-man roster was required for him to play again.

The Broncos also elevated safety Taylor Rapp and running back Cody Schrader from the practice squad for the Panthers game. Rapp was released Friday with the understanding he would be re-signed to the practice squad, then elevated. It was his third elevation, so he must be signed to the 53-man roster to play in another game after Sunday.

The NFL also announced Saturday that Uwazurike was fined $6,361 for a facemask penalty against Kansas City running back Kenneth Walker III in the first quarter.

stories.headline: Broncos' reserve defensive backs step up amid secondary injuries
stories.summary:
The Broncos (6-2) have won four straight games despite a run of injuries in the secondary, with reserves filling in effectively. The problems began late in the first half of a 24-14 loss at San Francisco on Oct. 4, when cornerback Pat Surtain II suffered a noncontact ankle injury and Riley Moss broke rib cartilage. Surtain missed 3 1/2 games and Moss 1 1/2.

Safety Taylor Rapp, a seven-year veteran who won a Super Bowl with the Los Angeles Rams, has spent much of the season on the practice squad and was elevated for two games. He is expected to play a key role Sunday at Carolina because starting safety Brandon Jones is out with a hamstring injury suffered against Kansas City. Star safety Talanoa Hufanga, who has missed three games with an ankle injury, is questionable. Devon Key and JL Skinner have also provided safety depth, while Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine have performed well at cornerback.

Rapp said he has never played on a team with a secondary this deep and credited the coaches and staff for acquiring and developing players. Coach Sean Payton stopped short of saying it is the deepest secondary he has had but said the performance of reserves comes back to drafting and preparing for a long season.

stories.headline: Avalanche return to Ball Arena to face Red Wings after two straight losses
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche host the Detroit Red Wings on Saturday evening at Ball Arena, the first meeting between the teams this season. Colorado is 9-6-2 and coming off a 7-2 loss at Columbus and a 3-2 overtime loss at Nashville. Detroit is 7-7-3 and has lost three of its last four.

Colorado leads the NHL with 53 five-on-five goals through 17 games. Nathan MacKinnon has 27 points, and Artturi Lehkonen leads the team with 12 goals. Defensive breakdowns and struggling special teams have offset that offense. Projected lines have Lehkonen, MacKinnon and Martin Necas together, with Mackenzie Blackwood expected to start in goal and Scott Wedgewood backing up.

Detroit's starting goaltender John Gibson is out again with a lower-body injury, leaving Daniil Tarasov in net. Lucas Raymond, Alex DeBrincat and Viktor Arvidsson have been productive offensively for the Red Wings. The teams once shared one of hockey's biggest rivalries, though they no longer play in the same conference.

topStory.headline: Gunman Kills Six in Shooting Attack in Krakow's Main Market Square; Three Relatives Found Dead at His Home
topStory.summary:
A gunman fired from a moving vehicle in Krakow's Main Market Square around 3 p.m. local time Saturday, killing six people and injuring at least 15 others, Polish authorities said. Police said the victims killed in the square were four women and two men. The suspect was shot by police a short distance from the initial violence and taken to a hospital. Police said he acted alone. Polish Defense Minister characterized the incident as a "terror attack."

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński identified the suspect as a Polish national in his mid-20s, reported by CBS News as 25, from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 93 miles northeast of Krakow. Kierwiński said he used an automatic rifle and held "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views, adding that "everything indicates he was fascinated by far-right ideologies." Krakow police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło told TVN24 that the gunman wore military-style fatigues and carried a military-type long gun, and that officers found numerous other weapon parts and ammunition in his car. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three of the suspect's relatives, a man and two women believed to be his parents and sister, were later found dead in his home, calling it the "next acts of this tragedy."

Two police officers were seriously wounded. Tusk named them as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Moranski and said they likely saved many lives while risking their own. Kierwiński said one officer was shot three times and underwent surgery. Four of the dead have been identified, though names were not released: three Polish nationals and one British citizen, according to Krakow police and the U.K. Foreign Secretary. An Interior Ministry spokesperson said injured foreign nationals include people from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and Britain. The U.S. State Department said it was not aware of any American citizens harmed.

Krakow declared a period of mourning, which the city said would run through Nov. 11 (CBS reported Wednesday). Mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city would remain open to visitors, stating, "The square will belong to us again." Tusk traveled from Warsaw to Krakow, and U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose condemned what he called a savage and murderous attack. Main Market Square is one of Poland's best-known commercial and tourist destinations, and the attack drew an international response.

Investigators continue to examine the suspect's background, his possible motives, and the circumstances of the deaths of his relatives, as well as how he obtained his weapons. Officials have emphasized his reported far-right ideology as a central line of inquiry. Following a police appeal for blood donations for one of the wounded officers, regional police said Sunday that Krakow's blood donation center was full and could accept no more donors, adding that public response exceeded expectations.
